subject: chemistry
title: Indicators and Colour
welcome_lead: Drop in some dye and watch acids and alkalis show their true colours.
meta_desc: Learn how universal indicator and litmus work in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now read the rainbow of universal indicator with confidence.

concepts.def: A substance that changes colour with pH.
Red in acid, blue in alkali.
Shows the full rainbow of colours for pH 0-14.
Universal indicator colour in strong/weak acid.
Universal indicator colour in weak/strong alkali.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Litmus is a simple indicator: red in acid, blue in alkali. It can't tell you exactly how acidic — just acid or alkali.

Red = acid, Blue = alkali.

Universal indicator shows a whole rainbow of colours. You compare the colour to a chart to read the pH.

Acid → red, orange, yellow. Neutral → green. Alkali → blue, purple.
Many plants contain natural indicators. Red cabbage juice turns pink in acid and green/yellow in strong alkali. You can make your own indicator at home!

mcqs.q: Is the oxidation state of an atom the same as its actual charge?
options: Benzene cannot react at all because it's too stable.
The oxidation state of an atom is always equal to the number of electrons it has.
The oxidation state of an atom is exactly equal to its real ionic charge in every compound.
Not necessarily — oxidation state is an accounting tool assuming all bonds are fully ionic; real charge is usually smaller.

mcqs.q: When an acid neutralises an alkali, what is the pH of the resulting solution?
options: Approximately 7 if equivalent amounts of strong acid and strong alkali react — but it varies with strength.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH exactly 7 regardless of the acid and base used.
Benzene cannot react at all because it's too stable.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition reactions?
options: Adding across a C=C would destroy the stable delocalised pi system; substitution preserves the aromatic ring.
Benzene cannot react at all because it's too stable.
Benzene contains three normal alternating double bonds and behaves like an alkene with three C=C.
Neutralisation always produces a solution with pH 0.
